section.title: Building the Tabernacle
section.sectionRationale: What God commanded in chapters 25 and 26 is now actually built. The people's generosity so overflows that Moses must restrain further giving, and Bezalel, Oholiab, and every skilled craftsman construct the tabernacle's curtains, coverings, frames, and veil exactly as the pattern required.
section.thesis: The skilled craftsmen begin the work with more than enough materials already given, and they construct the tabernacle's inner curtains, outer coverings, wooden frames, and dividing veil precisely as the LORD had commanded Moses.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the craftsmen begin work and the people's giving must be restrained; the ten inner curtains; the goat hair tent covering; the upright frames and crossbars; and the veil separating the two chambers.

units.label: More than enough
units.note: the people were restrained from bringing more

media.alt: Craftsmen surrounded by piles of gold and cloth
media.caption: The people bring so much that Moses must command them to stop giving.

verses.text: “So Bezalel, Oholiab, and every {{skilled|skilled}} person are to carry out everything commanded by the LORD, who has given them skill and ability to know how to perform all the work of constructing the sanctuary.”
Then Moses summoned Bezalel, Oholiab, and every skilled person whom the LORD had gifted, everyone whose heart stirred him to come and do the work.

They received from Moses all the contributions that the Israelites had brought to carry out the service of constructing the sanctuary. Meanwhile, the people continued to bring freewill offerings morning after morning,
so that all the skilled craftsmen who were doing all the work on the sanctuary left their work
and said to Moses, “The people are bringing more than enough for doing the work the LORD has commanded us to do.”

After Moses had given an order, they sent a proclamation throughout the camp: “No man or woman should make anything else as an offering for the sanctuary.” So the people were restrained from bringing more,
since what they already had was more than enough to perform all the work.

All the skilled craftsmen among the workmen made the ten curtains for the tabernacle. They were made of finely spun linen, as well as blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, with cherubim skillfully worked into them.
Each curtain was twenty-eight cubits long and four cubits wide; all the curtains were the same size.
And he joined five of the curtains together, and the other five he joined as well.
He made loops of blue material on the edge of the end curtain in the first set, and also on the end curtain in the second set.
He made fifty loops on one curtain and fifty loops on the end curtain of the second set, so that the loops lined up opposite one another.
He also made fifty gold clasps to join the curtains together, so that the tabernacle was a unit.

units.label: The outer coverings
units.note: goat hair, ram skins, fine leather

verses.text: He then made curtains of goat hair for the tent over the tabernacle, eleven curtains in all.
Each of the eleven curtains was the same size, thirty cubits long and four cubits wide.
He joined five of the curtains into one set and the other six into another.
He made fifty loops along the edge of the end curtain in the first set, and fifty loops along the edge of the corresponding curtain in the second set.
He also made fifty bronze clasps to join the tent together as a unit.
Additionally, he made for the tent a covering of ram skins dyed red, and over that a covering of fine leather.

units.label: The frames and crossbars
units.note: as the LORD had commanded Moses

verses.text: Next, he constructed upright frames of acacia wood for the tabernacle.
Each frame was ten cubits long and a cubit and a half wide.
Two tenons were connected to each other for each frame. He made all the frames of the tabernacle in this way.
He constructed twenty frames for the south side of the tabernacle,
with forty silver bases to put under the twenty frames, two bases for each frame, one under each tenon.
For the second side of the tabernacle, the north side, he made twenty frames
and forty silver bases, two bases under each frame.
He made six frames for the rear of the tabernacle, the west side,
and two frames for the two back corners of the tabernacle,
coupled together from bottom to top and fitted into a single ring. He made both corners in this way.
So there were eight frames and sixteen silver bases, two under each frame.
He also made five crossbars of acacia wood for the frames on one side of the tabernacle,
five for those on the other side, and five for those on the rear side of the tabernacle, to the west.
He made the central crossbar to run through the center of the frames, from one end to the other.
And he overlaid the frames with gold and made gold rings to hold the crossbars. He also overlaid the crossbars with gold.

units.label: The veil and the entrance curtain

verses.text: Next, he made the veil of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and finely spun linen, with cherubim skillfully worked into it.
He also made four posts of acacia wood for it and overlaid them with gold, along with gold hooks; and he cast four silver bases for the posts.
For the entrance to the tent, he made a curtain embroidered with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and finely spun linen,
together with five posts and their hooks. He overlaid the tops of the posts and their bands with gold, and their five bases were bronze.

skilled.gloss: Skilled or wise of heart, literally wise-hearted. This phrase links craftsmanship directly to wisdom, treating fine practical skill not as a lesser ability but as a genuine expression of God-given wisdom applied to physical work.

basic.context: This chapter records the actual construction beginning: so much material had already been given that Moses had to stop the people from bringing more. Bezalel, Oholiab, and the skilled craftsmen then build the tabernacle's inner curtains, outer coverings, wooden frames, and dividing veil exactly according to the pattern given back in chapters 25 and 26.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a straightforward historical record of construction matching earlier divine instruction almost word for word. Its significance lies less in hidden symbolism within each repeated detail and more in the striking fact of obedience: what God commanded is now, at last, actually done, faithfully and abundantly.
basic.originalLanguages: The craftsmen are repeatedly called chakham lev, wise or skilled of heart, a phrase that treats fine practical craftsmanship as a genuine form of wisdom, not a lesser, merely manual skill. The narrative's near word for word repetition of the earlier instructions underscores exact obedience to the pattern shown Moses.
basic.typology: The overflowing abundance that must be restrained anticipates the New Testament's vision of a church so generous in giving that need itself becomes rare, Acts 4:34. The precise correspondence between command and construction shows a pattern of faithful obedience that anticipates Christ's own perfect obedience to the Father's will.
basic.christ: Just as the tabernacle was built exactly as commanded, Jesus consistently declares that He does exactly what the Father commands Him, John 5:19, 8:29, the perfect fulfillment of faithful, obedient construction of God's purposes. The overflowing generosity here also anticipates the church's Spirit-filled generosity in Acts, itself a fruit of union with Christ.
basic.god: God's detailed instructions are met here with equally detailed obedience, showing that He cares as much about faithful execution as about the initial vision. His provision through the people's hearts is so abundant that restraint, not scarcity, becomes the problem, revealing the sufficiency of what He supplies for His own purposes.
basic.crossReferences: Acts 4:32-35 describes the early church's similar overflowing generosity, so that there was no needy person among them. John 5:19 and 8:29 show Jesus doing exactly what the Father commands, the perfect fulfillment of obedient construction. 1 Corinthians 3:10-15 speaks of building carefully on the foundation God has laid.
basic.oneStory: God's detailed pattern for His dwelling place is met with detailed, faithful obedience and such overflowing generosity that giving must be restrained. This pattern of abundant provision and exact obedience to God's design points forward to Christ's own perfect obedience to the Father and the church's Spirit-given generosity in building up God's true dwelling place.

context.literary:
Exodus 36 opens the last movement of the book's long tabernacle section. Chapters 25 to 31 give the instructions in seven speeches, each introduced by the words 'the LORD said to Moses,' Exodus 25:1, 30:11, 30:17, 30:22, 30:34, 31:1 and 31:12, and the seventh concerns the Sabbath. Chapters 32 to 34 tell of the calf, the intercession of Moses and the renewal of the covenant. Chapters 35 to 40 then carry out what was commanded. The two halves are hinged on the Sabbath, which closes the instructions in Exodus 31:12-17 and opens the execution in Exodus 35:1-3, so that the whole work of building is framed by the command to rest from work.

The first verse of the chapter actually completes the speech Moses began at Exodus 35:30, which is why the BSB keeps it inside quotation marks. Verses 1 to 7 then form a small narrative with its own tension and release: giving continues 'morning after morning,' verse 3; the craftsmen leave their work to report, verses 4 and 5; and a proclamation through the camp brings it to an end, verses 6 and 7. The unit is bracketed by 'all the work' in verse 1 and 'all the work' in verse 7.

From verse 8 the narrator retells Exodus 26 almost clause for clause, turning 'you are to make' into 'he made.' Set 'so that the tabernacle will be a unit,' Exodus 26:6, beside 'so that the tabernacle was a unit,' Exodus 36:13. The order has changed, though. The instructions began with the ark, Exodus 25:10, and moved outward from the throne of God toward the people. The construction begins with the house itself, curtains, coverings, frames and veil, before any furniture is made, which is the order in which a builder actually works. Directions about placement rather than making, such as where the ark, table and lampstand stand, Exodus 26:33-35, are left out here and held back for chapter 40, where Moses sets everything in its place, Exodus 40:3 and 40:21.
context.historical:
The scene is the camp at the foot of Sinai in the months after the covenant was renewed, Exodus 34:10, and before the tabernacle was raised 'on the first day of the first month of the second year,' Exodus 40:17. Much of the material came out of Egypt. On the night of the exodus the Israelites asked their neighbours for articles of silver and gold and for clothing, and 'in this way they plundered the Egyptians,' Exodus 12:35-36. Some of that very gold had recently gone into the fire for the calf, Exodus 32:2-4. The people who now give freely are the people who gave freely for an idol, and the account lets the reader feel the turn.

The materials mix the costly and the ordinary. Fine linen and yarn dyed blue, purple and scarlet were expensive fabrics, and the women of the camp spun them by hand, Exodus 35:25-26. Goat hair was the common cloth of tents, and the eleven goat hair curtains make a true tent over the linen dwelling. Ram skins dyed red and an outer covering, which the BSB renders 'fine leather' and footnotes as possibly the hides of large aquatic mammals, kept out the weather. Acacia, a hardy wood of the desert, supplied the frames, posts and crossbars.

The numbers let us picture the building. Twenty frames a cubit and a half wide on each long side give a length of thirty cubits; six frames plus the two corner frames at the rear give a width of about ten. The BSB footnote puts each frame at about fifteen feet tall. Each frame stood on two silver bases, and chapter 38 reveals that this silver came from the half shekel paid by every counted man, Exodus 38:25-27, so the sanctuary quite literally stood on the people's ransom money. Everything was made to be taken apart and carried. Later the Gershonites and Merarites transported the curtains, frames and bases on carts under the direction of Ithamar, Numbers 4:28, 4:33 and 7:6-8.
context.canonical:
The overflow of Exodus 36 sets a pattern for every later house of God. When David gathered materials for the temple the leaders 'gave willingly,' and the people rejoiced 'for they had given to the LORD freely and wholeheartedly,' 1 Chronicles 29:6-9, while David confessed, 'from Your own hand we have given to You,' 1 Chronicles 29:14. The master craftsman Solomon brought from Tyre was 'the son of a woman from the daughters of Dan,' 2 Chronicles 2:14, a quiet echo of Oholiab of Dan working beside Bezalel of Judah. After the exile the heads of families again 'gave freewill offerings to rebuild the house of God,' Ezra 2:68-69, and Haggai rebuked a generation content to live in paneled houses 'while this house lies in ruins,' Haggai 1:4.

In the New Testament Stephen recalls that the tabernacle 'was constructed exactly as God had directed Moses, according to the pattern he had seen,' Acts 7:44. Hebrews quotes the warning of Exodus 25:40 to show that the whole structure was 'a copy and shadow of what is in heaven,' Hebrews 8:5. John says that the Word 'made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14, with a verb drawn from the word for a tent. The veil made in verse 35 becomes in Hebrews 10:19-20 a picture of the body of Christ, the curtain through which a new and living way has been opened.

Paul, urging the Corinthians to finish their collection, reaches back into the wilderness and quotes the manna rule, 'He who gathered much had no excess, and he who gathered little had no shortfall,' 2 Corinthians 8:15, from Exodus 16:18. The same God who gave Israel bread morning by morning now receives His people's gifts morning after morning, Exodus 36:3. The story ends where the tabernacle points: 'the dwelling place of God is with man,' Revelation 21:3.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses writes so that Israel will know the tabernacle was not their idea, their design or their achievement, and yet that it was truly their work. Three things are pressed on the first hearers. First, the building rests on God's gifting: verse 1 says the LORD 'has given them skill and ability,' and verse 2 calls the workers those 'whom the LORD had gifted.' Second, it rests on willing hearts: the workers came because their hearts 'stirred' them, verse 2, and the givers brought 'freewill offerings,' verse 3. No one is conscripted and no tax is levied. Third, it rests on the pattern: the close repetition of Exodus 26 assures every later reader that what stood in the camp was what God had shown on the mountain, Exodus 25:9 and 25:40.

For a people who had just made an idol with their own gold to their own design, Exodus 32:4, this matters enormously. The calf was worship invented from below. The tabernacle is worship received from above and offered back with joy. Moses wants Israel to see that the forgiven people have become a giving people, and that God is pleased to dwell among them on His own terms, with nothing lacking and nothing added.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records what happened; it commands nothing directly. No reader is told to spin goat hair or cast silver bases, and churches are not told to build with these measurements. Some features carry forward, however, because the New Testament takes them up. Giving that is voluntary, prompted from the heart rather than squeezed out by pressure, is exactly what Paul asks for, 'not out of regret or compulsion,' 2 Corinthians 9:7. Gifts of skill given by God for building His house continue in the church, where each person uses 'whatever gift he has received to serve one another,' 1 Peter 4:10, and gifts are given 'to build up the body of Christ,' Ephesians 4:12.

The restraint of verse 6 is also description, but it instructs. Moses stopped the collection when the need was met instead of banking the surplus. That honesty about sufficiency is worth imitating by anyone who handles gifts given to God, even though the text lays down no rule about it.

debates.question: Why does the text repeat the tabernacle's specifications almost word for word from chapter 26 rather than simply summarizing the construction?

views.label: Emphasis on precise, faithful obedience
views.case: The repetition is the message. By turning each 'you are to make' of chapter 26 into 'he made,' the narrator lets the reader check the work against the plan line by line and find no gap. After the calf, where Israel 'turned aside quickly from the way' God commanded, Exodus 32:8, a record of exact correspondence shows a people restored to obedience. Chapter 39 makes the point explicit with its refrain, 'just as the LORD had commanded Moses.'

views.label: Ancient literary convention for building accounts
views.case: Others note that ancient building accounts commonly set a command and its execution side by side in nearly identical words, so the repetition may reflect the expected form of such a record as much as a special theological emphasis. On this view the form is simply how a faithful report of a sacred building was written.

views.label: Both, with a covenant purpose
views.case: A third reading holds the two together: Moses uses a familiar form, but places it after the breach and renewal of the covenant in chapters 32 to 34, so that the repeated wording becomes evidence that God's forgiven people are now building His house His way.

debates.bearing: Whatever its origin, the repetition works within Exodus to show exact correspondence between what God commanded and what Israel built, and its placement after the calf gives that correspondence the weight of repentance lived out.

debates.question: What were the 'frames' of the tabernacle walls: solid boards or open frameworks?

views.label: Solid boards
views.case: Older translations such as the King James Version render the word 'boards,' and the natural picture is a solid wooden wall: each unit ten cubits by a cubit and a half, overlaid with gold, verse 34, and bound together by five crossbars on each side, verses 31 to 33. The same Hebrew noun describes the deck of a ship in Ezekiel 27:6, a solid surface.

views.label: Open frames
views.case: Many modern translations, the BSB among them, render 'frames.' Each unit had 'two tenons connected to each other,' verse 22, which fits two uprights joined by rungs. Solid planks of that size would be very heavy for the Merarites to carry, Numbers 7:8, and an open framework would let the cherubim woven into the linen curtains, verse 8, be seen from inside rather than hidden behind wood.

debates.bearing: The text does not settle the question, and nothing theological hangs on it. Either way the walls were gold-covered acacia standing on silver, built to be taken down and carried, and lined inside with curtains full of cherubim.

study.originalLanguages:
The offerings of verse 3 are nedabah, 'freewill offerings,' from the root nadab, to be willing or to volunteer. The same root has run through the whole appeal: God asked for gifts from everyone 'whose heart compels him,' Exodus 25:2, and the people came 'whose hearts prompted them,' Exodus 35:29. The reflexive form of the verb describes the people who 'volunteer' for battle in Judges 5:2 and the leaders' 'willing response' in 1 Chronicles 29:9. The word leaves no room for coercion; what builds the sanctuary is gladly given.

The workers of verse 2 are those 'whose heart stirred him to come,' literally 'whose heart lifted him,' using the common verb nasa, to lift or carry. The identical expression describes the givers in Exodus 35:21. The picture is of a heart that rises and carries the person with it into the work.

In verse 6 the people 'were restrained from bringing more.' The verb is kala, to hold back or shut up. It is the word used when the flood ended and 'the rain from the sky was restrained,' Genesis 8:2. Here what has to be held back is not judgment but generosity. Verse 7 then says the materials were 'more than enough,' literally enough 'and to spare,' using a form of yatar, to be left over. The same verb describes the manna the Israelites 'left' until morning, which bred maggots, Exodus 16:19-20. In the wilderness, hoarded surplus rotted; here surplus is turned away because the need is met.

Two words for the building run side by side. The linen layer is the mishkan, 'tabernacle,' from shakan, to dwell, so its very name means dwelling place. The goat hair layer is the ohel, 'tent,' verse 14, 'curtains of goat hair for the tent over the tabernacle.' The dwelling and the tent are each joined by fifty clasps so that each becomes 'a unit,' verses 13 and 18, literally 'one.' The Septuagint renders the dwelling with skene, tent, the noun behind the verb John uses when the Word 'made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14.

The cherubim on the inner curtains and on the veil are 'skillfully worked,' verses 8 and 35, the phrase maaseh choshev, the work of a designer, from chashab, to think or devise. It echoes the gift given to Bezalel 'to design artistic works,' Exodus 35:32. The entrance curtain of verse 37 is different work, 'embroidered,' needlework rather than figures woven into the fabric. The two hangings also carry different names. The inner hanging is the paroket, 'veil,' a word kept for the partition before the ark, while the entrance curtain is a masak, a screen, from a root meaning to cover or shelter. The Septuagint uses katapetasma for the veil, and that is the word the Gospels use when 'the veil of the temple was torn in two,' Matthew 27:51, and the word Hebrews uses for the curtain through which Jesus has entered, Hebrews 6:19 and 10:20.

A final note on the Greek: the Septuagint arranges the material of these closing chapters of Exodus in a noticeably different order from the Hebrew, one of the larger differences between the two in the Pentateuch. The Hebrew order, followed by English Bibles, builds the house before the furniture.

typology.fulfillment: Cherubim once guarded the way to the tree of life, Genesis 3:24, and here they are woven into the curtain that bars the way to the ark. The veil taught Israel that God was near but not approachable at will. At the death of Jesus the veil of the temple 'was torn in two from top to bottom,' Matthew 27:51, and Hebrews says believers now enter 'by the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body,' Hebrews 10:19-20. The type falls short because the woven veil could only keep people out, while Christ's torn flesh brings them in, and He has gone ahead as 'our forerunner,' Hebrews 6:20.

typology.type: The tabernacle as God's dwelling among His people
typology.fulfillment: The linen dwelling was the place where the LORD chose to live among Israel, Exodus 25:8 and 29:46. John says the Word 'made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14, and Paul that in Christ 'all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form,' Colossians 2:9. Jesus called His own body the temple He would raise in three days, John 2:19-21. The escalation is from curtains and frames to a human body, from a symbol of presence to God Himself with us, Matthew 1:23. The tent fell short because it was temporary and could be defiled and abandoned; the risen Christ is 'the true tabernacle set up by the Lord, not by man,' Hebrews 8:2.

typology.type: The Spirit-gifted builders of the sanctuary
typology.fulfillment: Bezalel was filled 'with the Spirit of God, with skill, ability, and knowledge,' Exodus 31:3, and every worker in verse 2 was one 'whom the LORD had gifted.' In the New Testament the risen Christ gives gifts to His people 'to build up the body of Christ,' Ephesians 4:11-12, and in Him believers 'are being built together into a dwelling place for God in His Spirit,' Ephesians 2:22. The correspondence is clear, but the new covenant surpasses the old: then a few craftsmen built a tent, now every believer is gifted, 1 Corinthians 12:7, and the believers themselves are the living stones of the house, 1 Peter 2:5.

typology.type: The silver bases cast from ransom money, Exodus 36:24-30
typology.fulfillment: Every frame of the dwelling stood on silver that came from the half shekel paid by each counted man as 'a ransom for his life,' Exodus 30:12 and 38:25-27. God's house rested on a foundation of ransom. Peter says believers were redeemed 'not with perishable things such as silver or gold' but 'with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot,' 1 Peter 1:18-19. The pattern holds, since God's dwelling with sinners rests on a ransom paid, but the price has changed from metal to a life, and the ransom no longer needs paying at every census, because it was given 'once for all,' Hebrews 9:12.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first by the thing it builds. God told Moses to make a sanctuary 'so that I may dwell among them,' Exodus 25:8, and every curtain, clasp and frame in Exodus 36 serves that purpose. When John introduces Jesus he reaches for this very picture: 'The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us. We have seen His glory,' John 1:14. The glory that would fill the finished tabernacle, Exodus 40:34, is the glory John saw in the Son. Jesus made the link Himself when He spoke of 'the temple of His body,' John 2:21. The tabernacle was a true dwelling, but it was a tent pointing beyond itself; Hebrews calls Christ's ministry one carried out in 'the greater and more perfect tabernacle that is not made by hands,' Hebrews 9:11.

It leads to Christ through the veil. Verse 35 describes a curtain of blue, purple and scarlet with cherubim worked into it, hung between the Holy Place and the Most Holy Place. For centuries it told Israel that the way into God's presence was not yet open, a point Hebrews 9:8 draws out directly. When Jesus died, the veil of the temple was torn 'from top to bottom,' Matthew 27:51, torn from above, by God's hand rather than man's. Hebrews then identifies the curtain with 'His body,' Hebrews 10:20: the way in was opened when His flesh was torn. Believers now enter the Most Holy Place 'by the blood of Jesus,' Hebrews 10:19, with a confidence no Israelite worshiper could have had.

It leads to Christ by contrast with the builders. Moses was faithful in God's house, but Hebrews insists that 'Jesus has been counted worthy of greater glory than Moses, just as the builder of a house has greater honor than the house itself,' Hebrews 3:3. Bezalel built with gold from Egypt; Christ builds with people, 'and we are His house,' Hebrews 3:6. He promised, 'I will build My church,' Matthew 16:18, and He does it as Bezalel did, by the Spirit of God, giving gifts to His people for the work, Ephesians 4:11-12.

It leads to Christ in the giving that opens the chapter. The people brought so much that they had to be told to stop. Paul, raising a collection, grounds all Christian giving in a greater gift: 'though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, so that you through His poverty might become rich,' 2 Corinthians 8:9. Israel gave out of what God had given them from Egypt; the church gives out of what Christ gave by emptying Himself.

A caution is needed. The New Testament ties the tabernacle as a whole, and the veil in particular, to Christ. It does not assign a meaning to each loop, clasp and tenon, and readers do well not to invent one. The loops and clasps are there to show that God's dwelling was built with care and joined into one, not to hide a code.
study.god:
The chapter shows God as the giver of skill. Verse 1 speaks of the LORD 'who has given them skill and ability to know how to perform all the work,' and verse 2 calls the workers those 'whom the LORD had gifted.' Craftsmanship, weaving, casting and joinery are not outside God's interest; they come from Him. The Spirit of God who hovered over the waters at creation, Genesis 1:2, is the Spirit who filled Bezalel, Exodus 31:3. Isaiah says the same of the farmer, 'his God instructs and teaches him properly,' Isaiah 28:26. The God of Exodus is the Creator, and He equips human makers to make things for Him.

It shows a God who works through willing hearts. The same verse that says the LORD had gifted the workers says their hearts 'stirred' them to come, verse 2. Scripture holds these together without strain: God gives the ability and moves the will, and the people truly choose and truly give. God did not levy the tabernacle; He asked for it from those 'whose heart compels him,' Exodus 25:2, and the response overflowed. He wants gifts that are glad, 2 Corinthians 9:7.

It shows the sufficiency of God. The problem in verses 5 to 7 is too much, not too little. That surplus was not Israel's cleverness; the gold and linen came from Egypt because 'the LORD gave the people such favor in the sight of the Egyptians,' Exodus 12:36. God provides for what He commands. He does not need gifts, 'for the world is Mine, and the fullness thereof,' Psalm 50:12, yet He is pleased to receive them. 'The silver is Mine, and the gold is Mine,' Haggai 2:8, and He gives it so that His people may have the joy of giving it back.

It shows the holiness and nearness of God held together. The dwelling is in the middle of the camp, and God will live there among a people who had just broken His covenant. Yet at the heart of it hangs a veil, and behind the veil God is enthroned above the cherubim, Psalm 99:1. The cherubim woven into every inner curtain surround the priests with reminders of heaven's throne room. The God who comes near does not stop being holy, and the God who is holy does not refuse to come near.

It shows the condescension of God. The God of heaven agrees to live in a tent, and one designed to be packed up and carried. Centuries later He reminded David, 'I have moved about with a tent as My dwelling,' 2 Samuel 7:6. He travels with His people on their journey rather than waiting for them to arrive.

For worship, the chapter calls for gladness rather than grudging. The fitting response to such a God is a lifted heart, verse 2, that brings its best and is content when He says, 'It is enough.'

crossReferences.note: The instructions this chapter carries out. Reading the two chapters side by side shows that the curtains, coverings, frames, crossbars and veil match in number and measure, with 'you are to make' becoming 'he made.' What is missing, the placing of the ark and furniture, waits for Exodus 40.

The giving that produced the surplus of Exodus 36:3-7. Men and women whose hearts stirred them brought jewelry, yarn, skins, wood, stones and spices, and skilled women spun the linen and goat hair. Exodus 36 shows the result: more than the work could use.

The same people had brought their gold earrings to Aaron, who fashioned the calf. The contrast is deliberate: gold given for an idol of their own design, then gold given freely for a sanctuary of God's design. Exodus 36 shows forgiven people redirecting their gifts.

The temple's builders repeat the pattern of Exodus 36. The leaders gave willingly and the people rejoiced 'for they had given to the LORD freely and wholeheartedly.' In verse 14 David adds the theology beneath both collections: everything comes from God, and His people only give back what came from His hand.

Solomon's master craftsman, Huram-abi, is 'the son of a woman from the daughters of Dan,' skilled in gold, silver, bronze, yarn and fine linen. The temple is built by a craftsman whose lineage echoes Oholiab of Dan, who worked beside Bezalel on the tabernacle.

The reverse of Exodus 36. After the exile the people built paneled houses for themselves while the house of God lay in ruins. In the wilderness the people gave until they had to be restrained; in Haggai's day they had to be roused. The contrast measures a people's heart by its giving.

Paul quotes Exodus 16:18, the manna rule, in asking the Corinthians to give. His principle of equality, one people's surplus meeting another's need, reflects the same wilderness economy in which Exodus 36 sits: God provides, and His people share what He provides for His purposes.

Paul asks for giving that is decided in the heart, 'not out of regret or compulsion,' because God loves a cheerful giver. This is the New Testament form of the nedabah, the freewill offering of Exodus 36:3, which no one was forced to bring.

Stephen reminds the council that the tabernacle 'was constructed exactly as God had directed Moses, according to the pattern he had seen.' He draws on the testimony of Exodus 36 to 39 to argue that God's dwelling was always His own design, never a structure human hands could claim.

Hebrews quotes Exodus 25:40 to call the tabernacle 'a copy and shadow of what is in heaven.' The exact construction of Exodus 36 mattered because the building was an earthly picture of a heavenly reality, now entered by Christ as high priest.

The veil of Exodus 36:35 is read as a picture of Christ's body. Believers enter the Most Holy Place 'by the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body.' What the woven veil kept closed, His death has opened.

The Word 'made His dwelling among us,' with a verb built on the word for tent. John presents the incarnation as the reality the tabernacle of Exodus 36 anticipated, God living among His people, and adds that 'we have seen His glory,' the glory that filled the tabernacle in Exodus 40:34.

The end of the tabernacle story: 'the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them.' The tent of Exodus 36 was a portable, partial anticipation of this final and permanent presence of God with His people in the new creation.

study.oneStory:
The tabernacle answers a question that has hung over the Bible since Genesis 3: can human beings live in the presence of God again? In Eden God walked with the man and woman. After their rebellion He drove them out and 'stationed cherubim on the east side of the Garden of Eden' to guard the way to the tree of life, Genesis 3:24. Ever since, humanity has either run from God or tried to reach heaven on its own terms. At Babel people said, 'let us build for ourselves a city with a tower that reaches to the heavens, that we may make a name for ourselves,' Genesis 11:4. Exodus 36 is the opposite of Babel: a structure built not to make a name for its builders but at God's command, to His design, so that He might dwell among them.

The exodus itself was for this purpose. God brought Israel out of Egypt 'so that I might dwell among them,' Exodus 29:46. Redemption was never only rescue from slavery; it was rescue for fellowship. The golden calf nearly ended that hope, but God forgave, renewed the covenant, and now the building begins. Cherubim reappear, woven into the curtains and the veil, verses 8 and 35, still marking the boundary of holy space, but now at the centre of the camp rather than at the edge of a lost garden.

What begins here continues through the story. Solomon's temple replaces the tent, and its inner sanctuary is a perfect cube overlaid with gold, 1 Kings 6:20. Israel's sin drives the glory away; Ezekiel watches it depart from the temple, Ezekiel 10:18, and later sees it return, Ezekiel 43:4-5. Then the Word becomes flesh and makes His dwelling among us, John 1:14. At His death the veil is torn, Matthew 27:51, and at Pentecost the Spirit comes to dwell in a people, so that the church becomes 'a dwelling place for God in His Spirit,' Ephesians 2:22.

The story ends in a city. 'Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man,' Revelation 21:3. John sees no temple there, 'because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple,' Revelation 21:22, and the city is measured as a cube, 'all its dimensions were equal,' Revelation 21:16, as though the whole new creation has become the Most Holy Place. No veil hangs there and no cherubim bar the way. 'They will see His face,' Revelation 22:4. The curtains and frames of Exodus 36, raised by willing hands at the foot of Sinai, were a first sketch of that home.

quiz.q: Why did Moses eventually have to order the people to stop bringing offerings?

options.text: Because they had already brought more than enough to complete all the work.
options.note: Verses 5 to 7 explicitly state this reason.

options.text: Because the offerings were of poor quality.
options.note: The problem was abundance, not quality; the materials given were more than sufficient.

options.text: Because a famine required the materials be used for food instead.
options.note: No such famine or repurposing is mentioned; the issue was simply surplus for the building project.

options.text: The people never brought enough and construction was delayed.
options.note: Verses 5 through 7 explicitly describe abundance requiring restraint, not a shortage.

quiz.q: What was worked into both the ten inner curtains and the veil?

options.text: Cherubim, skillfully worked into the blue, purple, and scarlet yarn.
options.note: Verses 8 and 35 both describe cherubim worked into these two textiles.

options.text: Images of the sun and moon.
options.note: The described imagery is cherubim, not celestial bodies.

options.text: The names of the twelve tribes.
options.note: Tribal names appear on the priestly garments' stones, not woven into these curtains and the veil.

options.text: No imagery was included.
options.note: Verses 8 and 35 explicitly describe cherubim worked into both textiles.

quiz.q: What material were the tabernacle's outer coverings made from, layered over the goat hair tent?

options.text: Ram skins dyed red, and over that fine leather.
options.note: Verse 19 describes this exact layered covering.

options.text: Solid sheets of bronze.
options.note: Bronze was used for clasps, bases, and utensils, not as an outer tent covering.

options.text: A single layer of undyed cotton.
options.note: The coverings were specifically ram skins dyed red and fine leather, not undyed cotton.

options.text: No additional covering was made.
options.note: Verse 19 explicitly describes these layered coverings.

quiz.q: How were the tabernacle's acacia wood frames finished before assembly?

options.text: Overlaid with gold, with gold rings made to hold the crossbars.
options.note: Verse 34 describes this exact finishing of the frames.

options.text: Left as bare, unfinished wood.
options.note: The frames were specifically overlaid with gold, not left unfinished.

options.text: Painted with blue dye to match the curtains.
options.note: The frames were overlaid with gold, not painted with dye.

options.text: No finishing process is described.
options.note: Verse 34 explicitly describes the gold overlay and rings.

quiz.q: What material made up the bases for the veil's four posts?

options.text: Silver.
options.note: Verse 36 specifies four silver bases for the veil's posts.

options.text: Bronze.
options.note: Bronze bases were used for the entrance curtain's posts, verse 38, while the veil's posts specifically stood on silver bases.

options.text: Solid gold.
options.note: Gold overlaid the posts themselves and their hooks, but the bases underneath were silver, not solid gold.

options.text: No bases are mentioned for the veil's posts.
options.note: Verse 36 explicitly specifies four silver bases.

questions: The people gave so generously that Moses had to tell them to stop. What would it look like for your own giving, of time, money, or skill, to become this kind of overflowing rather than measured and cautious?
The craftsmen are called wise-hearted, treating their practical skill as true wisdom offered to God. Where do you undervalue practical, hands-on skill as a genuine form of worship and service to God?

The construction matched God's earlier instructions almost exactly, without deviation. Where in your own life are you tempted to improvise on God's revealed will rather than following it faithfully in the details?

Cherubim were woven into both the innermost curtains and the veil, a consistent reminder of guarded holiness throughout the structure. Where do you need a renewed sense of reverence in how you approach God, even in the ordinary parts of your life?

This chapter records patient, careful, detailed work, not dramatic events. How do you view the slow, unglamorous, faithful tasks in your own life, as lesser than the dramatic moments of faith, or as genuine acts of worship in their own right?

translationNotes.note: More than enough is a rare note of abundance in an ancient building account, where shortages of materials or labor were the more common concern; it reflects the depth of Israel's post-golden-calf generosity.

This section closely repeats the specifications given in Exodus 26:1-37 nearly verbatim, a literary pattern common in ancient Near Eastern building narratives to emphasize exact correspondence between divine command and human execution.

The veil described here corresponds exactly to the instructions of Exodus 26:31, underscoring that the same barrier separating the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place, later torn at Christ's death, was built precisely according to God's specified design.
